When something is described as sudorific, it means it causes sweating or promotes perspiration. That's the whole idea in a nutshell. If a thing — a medicine, a food, a plant, a treatment — has the ability to make your body produce sweat, that thing is sudorific.

Think of it this way: your body sweats for a reason. Sweating cools you down, releases certain waste products, and is one of the ways your body tries to fight illness. Anything that deliberately triggers or noticeably increases this sweating response is called sudorific.
What kinds of things can be sudorific?

The adjective "sudorific" is used to describe a wide range of things:

Medicines and drugs — Certain medications, especially older or traditional ones, are sudorific. Doctors or herbalists might prescribe them specifically to make a feverish patient sweat, because sweating helps break a fever and cool the body down.

Herbs and plants — Many plants have sudorific properties. Elderflower, yarrow, ginger, and boneset are classic examples used in herbal medicine for centuries. If you've ever had ginger tea when you were sick and noticed you started sweating, that's a sudorific effect in action.

Foods and spices — Spicy foods like chili peppers or cayenne are sudorific. When you eat something very spicy and your forehead starts to bead with sweat, that's because capsaicin (the compound that makes chilies hot) has a sudorific effect on the body.

Treatments and environments — A steam bath, a sauna, or a hot compress can also be described as sudorific because they cause the body to sweat significantly.

"Sudorific" is a formal, medical, and pharmacological term. You won't hear it much in everyday conversation — no one walks into a room on a hot day and says, "Wow, it's quite sudorific in here!" Instead, you're more likely to encounter it in:

  • Medical textbooks or pharmacology guides
  • Herbal medicine and naturopathy literature
  • Historical medical writing (it was very commonly used in older medical texts)
  • Academic or scientific articles about sweat glands, fever management, or plant-based medicine
How to use it in a sentence

Here are a few natural examples that show how the adjective works:

  • "The physician recommended a sudorific herb to help the patient sweat through the fever."
  • "Ginger is well known for its sudorific properties in traditional medicine."
  • "The sudorific effect of the hot steam room left everyone dripping."
  • "Doctors once relied heavily on sudorific treatments before modern fever-reducing drugs existed."
  • "The spicy soup had a surprisingly sudorific effect on everyone at the table."

Being sudorific is usually understood as a functional property — a quality that something has and exerts on the body. So when you call something sudorific, you're making a statement about its effect or capability, not just its temperature or intensity.

For example, a hot day might make you sweat, but we don't typically call a hot day "sudorific" in a medical sense — the word is more precisely reserved for things that actively trigger the sweat response through a physiological mechanism, like a drug stimulating the sweat glands, or a herb activating the body's heat-release system.

To summarize everything: sudorific is an adjective that means sweat-inducing. It's used to describe any substance, treatment, food, or agent that causes or promotes sweating in the body. The word belongs mostly to the world of medicine, pharmacology, and herbal science, where causing controlled sweating is sometimes a desired and therapeutic outcome — particularly for breaking fevers or cleansing the body. If you remember just one thing, remember this: sudorific = sweat-causing.
